day_narrative: A central and southern Plains supercell day produced very large hail, damaging winds, and a few tornadoes. Boundary placement and storm mergers governed local hazard intensity.

boundary_drivers: dryline|residual effective boundary|differential heating zone|central Plains front
day_narrative: West-central Texas was primed for intense supercells with giant hail. Large buoyancy and strong shear supported very large hail first, then clustering increased wind potential.

boundary_drivers: southward-surging cold front|southern High Plains dryline|Edwards Plateau low-level jet

boundary_drivers: Ohio Valley warm sector|low-level jet|warm front into the Mid South
day_narrative: Ohio Valley supercells developed in a moist, sheared warm sector after the prior Plains outbreak. A few strong tornadoes, very large hail, and damaging winds were all possible.

boundary_drivers: frontal zone|outflow-enhanced corridors|dryline into Texas and Oklahoma|low-level jet
day_narrative: A broad Moderate-risk outbreak stretched from the mid Mississippi and Ohio/Tennessee Valleys into the southern Plains. Numerous supercells produced very large hail and tornadoes before clusters and bows increased wind risk.

boundary_drivers: outflow boundary across the South|Texas dryline or warm sector|MCS cold pools
day_narrative: Intense Texas supercells produced very large hail, while a broader MCS and severe-wind corridor evolved into the Southeast. Tornado risk existed, but hail and damaging wind dominated.

boundary_drivers: prior-outflow-reinforced instability gradient|cold front|early-day MCS
storm_modes: fast squall line|bowing segments|QLCS mesovortices|small bowing clusters
day_narrative: An early-day MCS drove the main severe corridor across south Georgia and north Florida. Damaging winds were primary, with some QLCS tornado risk before the system moved offshore.

boundary_drivers: trailing outflow boundary in south Texas|Gulf Coast MCS track|sea-breeze or stationary boundary in Florida
day_narrative: Multiple severe corridors developed from south Texas and Louisiana to Florida. South Texas supercells produced hail while an organized bow-echo MCS crossed Louisiana with significant wind reports.

boundary_drivers: southern Plains instability plume|Kansas and Oklahoma border zone|subtle mesoscale boundaries
day_narrative: The southern Plains ENH risk centered on storms organizing near the Kansas and Oklahoma border. Large hail and severe gusts were expected, with narrow severe-wind swaths possible as multicells merged.

boundary_drivers: composite outflow boundary|central Texas to Louisiana instability gradient|storm-cluster cold pool
storm_modes: organized clusters|embedded bowing segments|supercells on south flank|squall line

boundary_drivers: outflow boundary in central Kansas|dryline|elevated mixed-layer plume|strengthening low-level jet
day_narrative: A Moderate-risk central Plains event emphasized potential derecho winds across Kansas and northern Oklahoma. Initial supercells produced giant hail and tornado potential, then storm clusters congealed into a severe line.

boundary_drivers: northeast Colorado upslope|frontal zone into southwest Nebraska|CAPE gradient
day_narrative: The central High Plains produced an evening supercell corridor from northeast Colorado into northwest Kansas and southern Nebraska. Very large hail and a cyclic tornado threat preceded a bowing transition.

boundary_drivers: warm front in Iowa and Wisconsin|prefrontal trough|dryline into Oklahoma and Texas|low-level jet
day_narrative: A Moderate-risk outbreak affected Iowa, Missouri, Illinois, Wisconsin, and adjacent areas. Fast-moving supercells produced a focused strong to potentially violent tornado threat, followed by a damaging squall line.

boundary_drivers: cold front|outflow or congealing storm boundary|Texas warm sector|Arkansas and Tennessee storm band
day_narrative: A long swath of severe storms extended from central Texas to the lower Great Lakes. Texas supercells had the largest hail and tornado risk, while clusters farther east emphasized damaging wind.

boundary_drivers: tail-end supercell complex|dryline from Oklahoma to Texas|low-level jet into Nebraska and Iowa|MCV over Kentucky and Tennessee
day_narrative: Dryline supercells occurred in Oklahoma and Texas while the central Plains MCS threat grew overnight. The most likely ENH hazard became damaging wind from Nebraska into Iowa.

boundary_drivers: morning bow-echo outflow boundary|cold front|dryline into Texas|Midwest instability plume
day_narrative: A messy multi-region day followed a severe morning bow echo over northern Illinois and southern Wisconsin. Its outflow complicated the Midwest risk while southern Plains storms developed in extreme buoyancy.

boundary_drivers: dryline from Texas to Oklahoma and Kansas|convective outflow|low-level jet|warm sector recovery
day_narrative: A central and southern Plains outbreak produced intense tornado and giant-hail potential from north Texas into Oklahoma and Kansas. Later upscale growth increased destructive wind potential into Missouri and Arkansas.

boundary_drivers: Ozarks to lower Ohio Valley warm sector|ongoing MCS or cold pool|open warm-sector initiation
day_narrative: Multiple severe rounds affected the Ozarks, Mississippi Valley, and Ohio/Tennessee Valleys. Discrete supercells produced strong tornado concern while an MCS brought a significant wind corridor.

boundary_drivers: residual outflow across Texas|central or southern High Plains dryline|Rio Grande MCS
day_narrative: Severe storms developed over much of Texas, with an early bowing MCS along the upper Texas coast and later supercells over west Texas. Residual outflow repeatedly focused renewed storms.

boundary_drivers: southern High Plains dryline|cold front|outflow ahead of the line
day_narrative: West and central Texas had the main ENH threat with supercells capable of baseball-size hail and a couple tornadoes. A linear MCS introduced a severe wind corridor and later QLCS development.

boundary_drivers: residual outflow boundary|lee trough or dryline|MCV from morning convection|High Plains terrain circulations
day_narrative: Scattered severe storms developed across the central and southern High Plains and spread into the adjacent Plains. MCV and outflow processes aided storm clusters while dryline and upslope initiation supported supercells.

boundary_drivers: remnant outflow boundary|central Plains MCS track|subtle baroclinic boundary in east Texas or Louisiana
day_narrative: A widespread Plains severe day produced multiple clusters, with the main risk evolving into a pronounced bowing MCS over Nebraska and Kansas. Farther south, an east Texas MCS added another wind and hail corridor.

boundary_drivers: southern Kansas or Oklahoma storm complex|central Oklahoma instability axis|cold front or outflow surge
day_narrative: Central and southern Oklahoma storms were expected to start as supercells with large hail before growing upscale into a severe-wind MCS. Tornado risk was secondary before the mode became linear.

boundary_drivers: central Plains storm cluster|cold-pool enhanced squall line|low-level jet into northeast Kansas
day_narrative: Central Plains supercells and clusters evolved into a cold-pool-enhanced squall line. Large hail was possible early, but damaging winds became the primary hazard as inflow strengthened.

boundary_drivers: central High Plains initiation zone|weak surface boundary|Kansas instability corridor
day_narrative: High Plains storms moved east-southeast into Kansas with a significant severe wind threat. Embedded supercells produced large hail early before consolidation into a larger MCS.

boundary_drivers: Upper Midwest warm sector|prefrontal zone|localized Minnesota boundary
day_narrative: Upper Midwest storms developed in a prefrontal warm sector with strong instability and shear. The main hazards were very large hail, damaging gusts, and a few tornadoes where storms stayed supercellular.

boundary_drivers: cold front from Iowa to Missouri and Illinois|High Plains dryline or front|warm well-mixed boundary layer
day_narrative: Severe storms organized from southern Iowa into northern Missouri and Illinois. Supercells with very large hail evolved toward a broken squall line or MCS with destructive wind potential.

boundary_drivers: remnant surface boundary in New England|cold front|warm-sector instability axis
day_narrative: The main ENH risk focused on New England and the Northeast where storms interacted with a remnant boundary. Damaging winds were common, while locally enhanced shear created a few-tornado risk.

boundary_drivers: effective warm front|occluded or cold front in Minnesota|strong warm advection zone
day_narrative: The Upper Midwest ENH risk centered on a possible destructive wind MCS from Minnesota into Wisconsin. Early supercells and elevated storms introduced hail and tornado potential before upscale growth.

boundary_drivers: deepening surface low|cold front or wind shift|northern High Plains instability plume
day_narrative: Northern and central High Plains storms organized into an MCS over the western Dakotas. Very large hail and a few tornadoes were possible early, while 75+ mph wind gusts became primary later.

boundary_drivers: cold front across the Northeast|prefrontal trough near I-95|Montana terrain or lee trough
day_narrative: A Northeast and Mid-Atlantic damaging-wind day unfolded along and ahead of a cold front, with additional Montana severe storms. Bowing clusters drove the main hazard, while hail was mainly early in supercells.

boundary_drivers: effective warm front from Kansas to Iowa|cold front|secondary surface low
day_narrative: Storms organized along an effective warm front from Kansas into Iowa and Missouri. A bowing MCS or QLCS produced severe winds and a few tornadoes, with hail mainly early.

boundary_drivers: eastern semicircle of Tropical Cyclone Beryl|convective rainbands|ArkLaTex to Arkansas shear corridor
day_narrative: Tropical Cyclone Beryl produced several tornado-risk corridors from east Texas into Louisiana and Arkansas. Low-topped supercells in outer rainbands were the main storm mode.

boundary_drivers: remnants of Beryl|northward-moving warm front|Ohio River shear corridor
day_narrative: Beryl's remnants shifted the tornado threat into the lower Ohio Valley. The main focus was near the Ohio River and warm front where low-level shear increased ahead of the remnant low.

boundary_drivers: remnants of Beryl|effective warm front across New York and New England|Mid-Atlantic cold front
day_narrative: Beryl's remnants contributed to a Northeast severe day, especially across upstate New York and New England. Discrete supercells near an effective warm front posed the primary tornado risk.

boundary_drivers: northern Plains instability gradient|Upper Mississippi Valley effective boundaries|High Plains terrain or dry boundary
day_narrative: Multiple clusters developed from the northern Plains into the Upper Mississippi Valley. Initial supercells produced hail and isolated tornado risk before upscale growth into MCSs drove wind overnight.

boundary_drivers: cold front|evolving MCS cold pool|Iowa-to-Illinois instability reservoir
day_narrative: A significant bowing MCS surged from Iowa into northern Illinois, the Chicago area, Indiana, and southern Michigan. Forecasts highlighted 75+ mph winds and embedded QLCS tornadoes.

boundary_drivers: MCV from prior severe MCS|cold front|central Plains outflow or MCS corridor
day_narrative: The day was driven in part by the prior night's MCS and embedded MCV moving into New York and New England. Damaging winds were the main concern, with tornadoes possible in stronger embedded storms.

boundary_drivers: southward-moving Nebraska storm cluster|central Plains boundary layer|High Plains initiation zone
day_narrative: The central Plains severe threat was mainly wind-driven as storms moved into a steep-lapse-rate boundary layer. The main uncertainty was whether a sustained cluster or bow would organize.

boundary_drivers: Dakotas dryline|mid-Missouri and Mississippi Valley MCS corridors|lower Ohio Valley instability gradient
day_narrative: A broad multi-region severe day produced damaging-wind swaths from the Midwest into the Tennessee Valley and southern Appalachians, with additional Plains supercells. MCS corridors dominated the ENH hazard.

boundary_drivers: central or northern Plains storm clusters|MCS cold pools|Midwest instability corridor

boundary_drivers: Ohio-to-New Jersey convective corridor|Debby coastal rainbands|Montana and Wyoming shortwaves|Arizona easterly flow
day_narrative: Separate severe regimes affected Ohio to New Jersey, the Debby-affected Carolinas, Montana/Wyoming, and Arizona. The ENH corridor was mainly wind-driven from northern Ohio into New Jersey.

boundary_drivers: eastern Wyoming shortwave|front or boundary across South Dakota and Minnesota|low-level jet into southeast South Dakota
day_narrative: Severe storms extended from the northern High Plains into Minnesota and Wisconsin. Initial supercells produced hail and a couple tornadoes before bow-echo MCSs became the main wind threat.

boundary_drivers: Dakotas baroclinic zone|low-level warm advection corridor|shortwave trough
day_narrative: Dakotas supercells formed ahead of an evening shortwave and strengthening low-level jet. Very large hail and a tornado or two were possible early before hail and wind became more dominant.

day_narrative: The day combined a Francine-remnant tornado threat over the central Gulf states with a High Plains severe-wind and hail event. Northern High Plains storms were supercellular, while Alabama had isolated tornado potential.

boundary_drivers: Front Range and High Plains upslope|central or southern Rockies terrain circulations|leading squall line
day_narrative: A High Plains wind event developed from New Mexico and Colorado into western Nebraska and Kansas. Scattered to numerous severe gusts were expected, with hail secondary.

storm_modes: low-topped supercells|rainband supercells|bands of rotating storms

boundary_drivers: warm front|cold front|northeast Texas to Ozarks warm sector|prior outflow or recovery zones
day_narrative: The severe focus shifted from north Texas and eastern Oklahoma into Arkansas, Missouri, and the mid Mississippi Valley. Discrete supercells produced the greatest tornado concern, including strong tornado potential.

boundary_drivers: frontal band over west Texas|low-level jet|northward edge of surface-based instability
day_narrative: A late-season nocturnal line developed from west Texas into southwest Oklahoma. Damaging winds were expected first, with tornado potential increasing as the line accelerated into stronger low-level shear.

boundary_drivers: southeast Texas warm sector|midlevel shortwave ascent|Louisiana low-level jet corridor
day_narrative: Southeast Texas supercells produced the day's highest tornado potential, including a possible strong tornado or two. The severe threat spread into Louisiana with broken lines and clusters.

boundary_drivers: cold front|low-level jet and moist axis|confluence bands|central Gulf Coast warm sector
day_narrative: A late-December southern severe outbreak evolved from Texas into the lower Mississippi Valley and central Gulf Coast. The forecast called for long-track strong tornadoes and severe wind with a QLCS likely preceded by supercells.

boundary_drivers: surging cold front|warm front over central LA/MS|pre-frontal confluence bands|intense low-level jet

boundary_drivers: slow northward-moving warm front|surface cold front|Gulf moisture axis

Early precipitation and shallow cool air made the northward recovery of surface-based instability a key forecast issue.

boundary_drivers: surface cold front|baroclinic zone on warm-return edge|pre-frontal warm sector

The main uncertainty was how long discrete or semi-discrete storms could mature ahead of the line.

boundary_drivers: advancing cold front|warm/moist advection zone|southern Plains shortwave trough
day_narrative: Thunderstorms developed across the southern and central Plains during the evening and expanded overnight. The timing of nocturnal initiation and upscale growth was the main challenge.

boundary_drivers: cold front|warm front|strongly forced pre-frontal zone

storm_modes: broken squall line|embedded circulations|low-CAPE line segments

Instability was modest in places, so recovery ahead of ongoing convection was important.

boundary_drivers: dryline|deep surface low|Pacific/cold frontal wind shift|low-level confluence axis

boundary_drivers: ongoing Ohio Valley squall line|lower Mississippi Valley frontal zone|convective outflow/cold pool
day_narrative: The day featured an ongoing Ohio Valley squall line and a separate lower Mississippi Valley severe episode later in the evening. Damaging winds were the primary hazard, with a couple of tornadoes possible where line segments interacted with richer instability. Convective timing and whether downstream air masses could recover controlled the magnitude of the ENH threat.

boundary_drivers: squall-line cold pool|trailing cold front|convective outflow

Cloud cover and prior convection modulated recovery, but the cold pool and line propagation sustained the ENH wind threat.

boundary_drivers: Kansas/Oklahoma dryline|northwest Kansas surface low|warm front|cold front
day_narrative: A southern and central Plains dryline/front setup supported isolated evening supercells with very large hail and a conditional tornado risk. Later, increasing ascent and the low-level jet favored a more organized line or cluster across Kansas and Oklahoma. Timing of initiation, cap erosion, and nocturnal mode transition were key uncertainties.

boundary_drivers: elongated baroclinic corridor|warm front|outflow-modified boundaries|low-level jet

boundary_drivers: stalled frontal zone|rain-reinforced baroclinic zone|remnant outflow boundaries

Boundary placement and whether storms remained on the warm side of the baroclinic zone were central to the forecast.

boundary_drivers: ArkLaTex warm-sector boundary|warm front|slow-moving frontal corridor

Hail and damaging winds remained important as storms clustered and moved northeast along the boundary.

boundary_drivers: surface boundary from the Sabine Valley to Tennessee|front/outflow corridor|pre-frontal warm sector

boundary_drivers: maturing mid-latitude cyclone|cold front|upper low/vorticity maxima

boundary_drivers: weak shortwave trough|retreating warm front|nocturnal low-level jet

Later elevated storms persisted but became less organized with time.

boundary_drivers: surface cold front|Red River/baroclinic boundary|outflow-modified inflow corridor
day_narrative: North-central Texas into southeast Oklahoma became the focus for a late-day and nocturnal supercell tornado threat. Upscale growth into an MCS/QLCS later shifted the hazard toward severe winds and QLCS tornadoes.

storm_modes: line with embedded supercells|QLCS|discrete storms near warm front

The event had both embedded-line and supercell character.

boundary_drivers: effective warm front/outflow boundary|dryline|differential heating zone|central/southern Plains lee trough
day_narrative: Central and southern Plains convection focused on boundaries from eastern Colorado and southwest Kansas into western Oklahoma, the Panhandles, and west Texas. boundary_drivers: west/east-oriented outflow boundary|southern High Plains lee trough|nocturnally strengthening low-level jet

Later clustering and storm interactions complicated longevity and wind potential.

boundary_drivers: Upper Midwest frontal zone|northeast Kansas storm cluster|southern Plains dryline
day_narrative: Multiple severe corridors evolved from the Upper Midwest into the central and southern Plains. Supercells produced large to very large hail and increasing tornado potential, including localized strong-tornado risk, while northern storms tended to grow upscale into linear clusters. The day is best classified as multi-region and multi-mode rather than a single-boundary event.

boundary_drivers: remnant outflow boundary|southern Plains storm cluster|Ohio Valley prior MCS corridors

day_narrative: Multiple storm clusters affected the southern Plains and the Ohio Valley. In north Texas and southern Oklahoma, an intense cluster with embedded supercells moved into an environment near a remnant outflow boundary, supporting large hail, significant wind, and localized tornado potential. Farther east, prior MCSs left pockets of recovery for additional damaging-wind clusters.

boundary_drivers: large organized MCS|substantial cold pool/wake low|warm front in southern Illinois/Indiana|outflow boundary
day_narrative: A large, organized MCS moved from southeast Oklahoma and northeast Texas toward Arkansas and the Mississippi Valley. Its cold pool and wake low supported damaging winds and a few embedded tornadoes, while separate warm-front and west Texas storms posed more localized hail/tornado threats. The dominant signature was forward-propagating MCS wind.

boundary_drivers: broad frontal zone|convectively modified front|southward-sagging boundary|cell cold pools
day_narrative: A broad, messy severe-weather day stretched from Texas and Louisiana into the Tennessee and Ohio Valleys. Storms developed along a convectively modified frontal zone, with very large CAPE supporting hail in Texas and numerous clusters/bowing segments producing damaging winds farther east. The setup was multi-region and multi-mode, with outflow placement and cold-pool amalgamation important.

boundary_drivers: southern High Plains lee trough|warm front|stationary front in the Mid-Atlantic|sea breeze boundary
day_narrative: The main ENH corridor centered on southern High Plains supercells during the evening and night, with very large hail and 70+ mph wind potential. Additional, more localized severe storms occurred along Mid-Atlantic, Dakotas, and Florida boundaries. The southern Plains tornado risk increased with time as supercells interacted with the warm front and low-level jet.

boundary_drivers: surface warm front|pre-frontal boundary|squall line|cold front/outflow boundary
day_narrative: Supercells were ongoing along and near a warm front across Texas, with a favorable environment extending into Louisiana. The day evolved into a mixed discrete and line/cluster event with large hail, damaging winds, and a few potentially strong tornadoes. Multiple other regions had secondary hail and wind threats, but east/southeast Texas into Louisiana was the main ENH focus.

boundary_drivers: occluded front|cold front|dryline feature|surface convergence zones
storm_modes: semi-discrete supercells|arcing band of supercells|MCS with embedded supercells|line segments
day_narrative: A deep upper low and occluded/cold frontal system produced a widespread severe event from the upper Mississippi Valley into the Great Lakes. Initial supercells brought strong tornado and very large hail potential, then storms merged into lines/MCSs with significant wind, especially into lower Michigan and Indiana. A secondary overnight hail/wind threat developed from Arkansas toward the Tennessee Valley.

boundary_drivers: seasonally deep cyclone|surface cold front|warm sector boundaries|dryline/frontal zone
day_narrative: A regional outbreak continued across the mid-Mississippi, Ohio, and Tennessee Valleys. Intense supercells produced strong, potentially long-track tornadoes and very large hail, with damaging winds increasing as storms clustered. The strongest corridor shifted from Missouri/Arkansas into Kentucky, Tennessee, and adjacent states during the evening.

boundary_drivers: southern Plains dryline/frontal zone|retreating warm front|remnant MCS/outflow corridors
day_narrative: The main severe focus was the southern Plains, where extreme buoyancy and shear supported supercells with very large hail, damaging winds, and a couple of tornadoes. Earlier and later MCS activity complicated the setup and also produced damaging winds farther east. Oklahoma, north Texas, and the ArkLaTex were the key all-hazards corridors.

boundary_drivers: dryline|warm front|central High Plains upslope/baroclinic corridor|outflow-modified boundaries
dominant_hazards: strong to intense tornadoes|very large hail|damaging wind
day_narrative: Central and southern Plains supercells were capable of all severe hazards, including several strong to intense tornadoes. Northwest Oklahoma into southwest Kansas and the central High Plains had the most concerning tornado/hail environment, while mergers and clusters gradually complicated storm mode. The day retained a classic discrete supercell signal despite localized outflow modulation.

boundary_drivers: dryline|warm front|QLCS gust front|Ozark/Red River severe corridor
dominant_hazards: strong tornadoes|widespread damaging wind|very large hail
day_narrative: A significant severe episode continued across the south-central states. Earlier discrete supercells produced giant hail and strong tornado potential, then a broad southwest-northeast QLCS with embedded supercells maintained strong tornado and significant wind potential from Oklahoma/Arkansas toward the Ozarks. The balance between discrete storm intensity and linear upscale growth defined the day.

boundary_drivers: cold front|warm-sector instability axis|ongoing convective line|southern Appalachians boundary zone
day_narrative: The main severe risk persisted from eastern Tennessee into Alabama and northwest Georgia. A line and associated embedded storms produced scattered damaging winds, a few tornadoes, and isolated large hail as activity spread east. Several MDs highlighted tornado potential within increasingly favorable low-level shear before the threat weakened overnight.

boundary_drivers: southwestward-drifting outflow boundary|baroclinic gradient|Red River/southern Plains boundary|Florida sea breeze
dominant_hazards: large to very large hail|damaging wind|tornadoes
day_narrative: Morning storms over Oklahoma left an outflow boundary that drifted into northwest Texas and the Low Rolling Plains. New storms along that boundary and baroclinic gradient produced large to very large hail and damaging winds, with a few tornadoes possible. Later clustering into a small MCS shifted the threat toward severe wind.

boundary_drivers: stationary effective warm front/outflow boundary|remnant MCS from Oklahoma/ArkLaTex|southern Plains shortwave trough
day_narrative: The evening severe focus shifted to the southern Plains, especially Oklahoma, where all hazards were possible along an effective warm front/outflow boundary. Earlier MCS remnants also propagated across Alabama and Mississippi, prompting downstream probability adjustments. The day was therefore strongly outflow and MCS modulated.

boundary_drivers: frontal zone|multiple outflow boundaries|southern Plains shortwave trough|MCS cold pools
day_narrative: Southern Plains storms again dominated the ENH day, with very large hail, severe winds, and a few tornadoes most concentrated in Oklahoma and Texas. Elevated storms grew upscale into an MCS while additional supercells formed near the Caprock and along frontal zones. Multiple boundaries and storm interactions governed the timing and hazard transition.

boundary_drivers: rapidly modifying remnant outflow|south-central Texas MCS/QLCS cold pool|High Plains trough
day_narrative: South-central Texas storms initiated along a rapidly modifying remnant outflow boundary. Early supercells supported very large to giant hail and tornado potential before an emerging MCS/QLCS produced significant to destructive wind gusts. The day is best classified as outflow-driven supercells transitioning into forward-propagating MCS wind.

boundary_drivers: southward-moving cold front|west/central Texas boundary|ArkLaTex surface low/shortwave
day_narrative: West and central Texas severe weather centered on an intense supercell and possible additional storms along a southward-moving front. Large to very large hail, significant gusts, and a couple of tornadoes remained possible, with some chance of upscale growth if coverage increased. A secondary ArkLaTex-to-Tennessee Valley threat was tied to modest instability and stronger wind profiles.

boundary_drivers: deepening surface cyclone|quasi-stationary front|trailing cold front|warm-front corridor
day_narrative: A surface low tracking along a quasi-stationary front supported a Mid-Atlantic and Carolinas severe corridor. Damaging winds were the dominant hazard, but low-level shear near the warm front supported a few tornadoes from Virginia toward the Tidewater and Carolinas. Western extent was limited as the surface low and cold front passed.

boundary_drivers: pronounced High Plains boundary|MCV over Minnesota|surface cold front|outflow/gust front
day_narrative: The main ENH corridor was the southern High Plains into western Kansas, where an organizing cluster along a boundary was expected to produce 60-75 mph winds and localized 75-90 mph gusts. A separate MCV over Minnesota also produced a shorter-lived severe wind threat. Hail and an isolated tornado were secondary hazards during the transition from storms to MCS.

boundary_drivers: High Plains shortwave|increasing low-level jet|western Oklahoma/southern Kansas boundary|weak MCV in the Northeast
dominant_hazards: very large to giant hail|tornadoes|damaging wind
day_narrative: Southern and central Plains supercells produced several tornadoes, possibly strong, and large to giant hail. A low-level jet strengthened ahead of a weak shortwave, supporting an evening corridor from western Oklahoma into southern Kansas while some storms grew upscale into an MCS. The Northeast had a smaller MCV-related severe threat.

boundary_drivers: lee trough|southern Rockies/High Plains moisture axis|cold front/outflow boundaries
day_narrative: A corridor from southeast Colorado into central Oklahoma supported supercells and one or two organizing clusters. Large hail and damaging winds were the main hazards, with a couple tornadoes possible during the supercell phase. Later, storms organized into a squall line across southern Kansas and Oklahoma with severe wind and embedded tornado potential.

boundary_drivers: morning MCS/MCV|cold pool|remnant outflow|dryline/outflow intersection in Texas
storm_modes: mature MCS|bowing line|embedded tornado circulations|isolated supercells
day_narrative: An MCS and associated MCV moved from the Mid-South into the Southeast, maturing into a damaging-wind-producing bowing system. The cold pool trimmed the western risk but sustained a corridor of wind damage and isolated tornado potential into Alabama, Georgia, and the southern Appalachians. Additional conditional supercell threats existed near High Plains and Texas outflow intersections.

boundary_drivers: diffuse baroclinic boundary|cold front|southern Plains outflow/frontal zone|low-level jet
day_narrative: Supercells and clusters from the Texas Panhandle into the Red River Valley were expected to consolidate into a prominent MCS. The wind threat increased markedly as merging storms developed bowing structure, with derecho potential and 80-100 mph gusts in northern Texas and southern Oklahoma. Large hail and tornadoes were important early, but widespread wind became dominant overnight.

boundary_drivers: central/southern Montana baroclinic zone|High Plains upslope flow|residual outflow/differential heating zone|Lower Mississippi cold pool
dominant_hazards: large to very large hail|damaging wind|tornadoes
day_narrative: The greatest severe concentration was across central and southern Montana, where supercells produced large to very large hail, severe gusts, and a couple tornadoes. Separate High Plains and lower Mississippi/Tennessee Valley clusters produced damaging winds, with outflow boundaries influencing storm placement. The setup was multi-region, but High Plains/northern Rockies supercells were the primary signal.

boundary_drivers: low-amplitude wave over Montana|northern High Plains baroclinic zone|southern High Plains terrain/upslope flow
day_narrative: Severe storms spread from Montana into northeast Wyoming and the western Dakotas, with large hail early and increasing severe wind as storms organized. Additional severe storms occurred across the central and southern Plains. The main ENH signal was supercells growing upscale into clusters with potential severe wind swaths through the night.

boundary_drivers: central Plains boundary|surface cyclone/front|MCS cold pool|low-level jet
day_narrative: Scattered severe storms developed across the northern and central Plains into the Upper Mississippi Valley. Early supercells brought hail and tornado potential, but severe wind became more prominent as storms grew into clusters and MCSs. The ENH area shifted south and east with evolving boundaries and cold-pool propagation.

boundary_drivers: surface front/composite outflow|strengthening low-level jet|southern Kansas/northern Oklahoma boundary
day_narrative: Southern Kansas and northern Oklahoma became the primary focus for swaths of damaging winds, some over 80 mph, with large hail and a couple tornadoes. Storms organized along a surface front/composite outflow as the low-level jet strengthened, favoring small bows and MCS evolution. Earlier supercells along the boundary added localized tornado and large-hail risk.

boundary_drivers: well-developed QLCS|MCV/shortwave over Missouri/Illinois|low-level confluence axis|outflow boundary in southern Plains
day_narrative: A well-developed QLCS with embedded bows tracked across Indiana and southern Lower Michigan toward Ohio, producing scattered to numerous damaging winds and tornado potential. Farther south, new storms along confluence and outflow boundaries from the lower Ohio Valley into the southern Plains added hail and wind risk. The event was strongly MCV/MCS driven.

boundary_drivers: weak cold front/upper trough|Blue Ridge terrain initiation|southeast outflow boundary|northern Plains dryline
day_narrative: The main severe corridor extended across the Mid-Atlantic into parts of the Northeast, where moderate buoyancy and sufficient shear supported organized clusters and line segments. Damaging winds were the primary hazard, with isolated hail and brief tornadoes possible. A separate northern Plains/Upper Midwest nighttime hail and wind risk developed along the stronger westerlies.

boundary_drivers: northern Plains shortwave trough|MCS cold pool|bow-echo apex|pre-MCS supercells
day_narrative: A significant swath of severe winds developed from the northern Plains into the upper Mississippi Valley. Supercells and multicells grew upscale into a mature bow echo/derecho, with 75-100+ mph gusts and mesovortex tornado potential. The MCS wind hazard was dominant, though very large hail and tornadoes occurred with early supercells.

boundary_drivers: Southeast cold pool/outflow mergers|southwest Wisconsin warm front|effective frontal boundary|northern High Plains terrain boundary
storm_modes: loosely organized MCS|embedded supercells|low-topped supercells|multicell clusters
day_narrative: Two main severe regimes shared the day. In the Southeast, outflow mergers consolidated a cold pool and supported a loosely organized MCS with damaging winds and hail. In southwest Wisconsin and nearby areas, supercells along a warm front produced tornadoes before trending more linear.

day_narrative: Northern Plains supercells developed along the northern edge of strong buoyancy across North Dakota and nearby areas. Later clustering introduced a more wind-dominant threat.

boundary_drivers: progressive northern High Plains shortwave|organized MCS cold pool|Black Hills/northern High Plains boundary|Tropical Storm Chantal rainbands
storm_modes: upscale-growing MCS|small MCS/supercell|high-based clusters|low-topped tropical rainband cells
day_narrative: The northern High Plains severe threat was dominated by an upscale-growing cluster/MCS moving from southeast Montana and northeast Wyoming into western South Dakota. Severe wind gusts were the main hazard, with isolated large hail in stronger storms. A separate low-end tropical rainband tornado threat existed near Tropical Storm Chantal along the Carolina coast.

boundary_drivers: surging outflow boundary|central High Plains upslope flow|cold front|weak Midwest/OH Valley boundaries
day_narrative: The central and northern Plains severe threat involved storms developing along outflow and upslope boundaries, then consolidating into one or more damaging-wind clusters. Large hail and a brief tornado were possible during the supercell phase, but severe wind became the main nighttime hazard. Farther east, scattered pulse and multicell storms produced more isolated damaging gusts.

boundary_drivers: northern/central Plains moisture gradient|low-level jet focus|Mid-Atlantic shortwave/front|northern Rockies shortwave
day_narrative: Severe wind and isolated large hail were possible in both the northern/central Plains and the Mid-Atlantic/Southeast. Confidence in a farther-south Plains corridor depended on whether storms moving out of the Nebraska Panhandle could organize with the low-level jet. The event was multi-region, with damaging wind the primary hazard.

boundary_drivers: MCV over southern Minnesota/western Wisconsin|surface low near Nebraska/Colorado border|warm/moist central Plains corridor|south flank of MCV
day_narrative: A midlevel MCV over the Upper Midwest interacted with a moist, unstable warm sector to produce renewed severe storms from Iowa into the Midwest. Farther west, central Plains storms developed near the surface low and later grew into a complex. Large hail and a couple tornadoes were possible early, with damaging winds increasing as storms organized.

boundary_drivers: warm-front-like baroclinic zone|reinforcing residual showers/clouds|central High Plains post-frontal boundary|Upper Midwest cold front
day_narrative: A sharpened warm-front-like zone from the lower Missouri Valley into the Midwest was the main severe focus. Storms near this boundary produced damaging wind, hail, and some tornado potential, while clusters later moved into the Great Lakes. Additional severe storms occurred across the central and southern High Plains and Upper Midwest.

boundary_drivers: cold front|South Dakota/Nebraska instability corridor|organized linear MCS|Upper Midwest front
day_narrative: An organized linear MCS became established from eastern South Dakota into central Nebraska. Scattered severe gusts, some 75+ mph, and large hail were probable as the system moved east-southeast into Iowa and southeast Nebraska. Other severe wind pockets occurred in the Upper Midwest, Wyoming, and southeast Arizona, but the Plains MCS drove the ENH classification.

boundary_drivers: Upper Mississippi Valley MCS|ridge-embedded perturbations|MCS gust front/outflow|northern Plains instability axis
day_narrative: An Upper Mississippi Valley MCS with intense embedded multicells and supercells produced a severe-wind threat into the night. Hail and localized tornado potential accompanied the strongest embedded storms, while the system gradually weakened toward Iowa. A separate, more isolated northern Plains severe threat remained secondary.

boundary_drivers: South Dakota/Nebraska border storm corridor|larger-scale damaging-wind MCS evolution|Montana storm complex
day_narrative: A significant damaging-wind corridor evolved from southeast South Dakota into southern Minnesota and northern Iowa. Earlier tornadic supercells transitioned into a complex mixture of modes, then larger-scale wind damage became the primary concern as cells filled in and merged. Hail and isolated tornadoes remained possible but were secondary to severe wind.

boundary_drivers: northern Plains warm front|Montana storm clusters|North Dakota weak surface boundary|steep lapse-rate/moisture corridor
dominant_hazards: significant severe wind|large to very large hail|tornadoes
day_narrative: Northern Plains storms organized across Montana into North Dakota during the evening and night. The downstream environment was volatile, supporting one or more swaths of significant severe winds along with large to very large hail and a few tornadoes. Elevated storms along the warm front complicated mode and timing but still supported severe potential.

boundary_drivers: convectively reinforced baroclinic zone|east Oklahoma/west Arkansas differential heating corridor|midlevel vorticity maximum
day_narrative: Eastern Oklahoma into western Arkansas became the focused severe corridor as heating occurred along and south of a convectively reinforced baroclinic zone. Supercells and clusters posed a few tornadoes, one or two potentially strong, along with scattered damaging winds and hail. The key forecast issue was storm development and interaction with the reinforced boundary.

boundary_drivers: surface low moving from Kansas toward Lake Michigan|warm front across Missouri/Illinois/Indiana|surging dryline into Missouri|shortwave trough
storm_modes: early elevated storms|discrete to semi-discrete supercells|supercell cluster

day_narrative: A compact cool-season Midwest/OH Valley setup relied on modest moisture returning beneath strong flow aloft. Outlooks and MDs emphasized supercells near the warm front and dryline, with large hail and tornadoes possible despite limited buoyancy. Later MDs confirmed discrete and clustered supercells, including a strong-tornado concern, while also noting uncertainty from poor thermodynamics.

boundary_drivers: southern High Plains dryline|lee cyclone over eastern Colorado|northward-moving warm front|low-level jet
storm_modes: initial discrete supercells|supercell clusters|late bowing structures|overnight elevated storms north of the warm front
day_narrative: The southern High Plains risk hinged on dryline initiation into an improving moist sector. Forecasts consistently favored a few supercells with very large hail and tornado potential, then clustering or bowing structures as the low-level jet strengthened. Capping and weak forcing limited confidence in storm number and timing, especially before evening.

storm_modes: initial supercells|bowing clusters|squall line|elevated hail storms north of the front
day_narrative: A broad Plains-to-Midwest severe day had several foci, including a cold front/warm front zone in the central Plains and Midwest and a conditional southern Plains dryline. The outlook raised tornado probabilities near the surface low/warm-front interface while also expecting bowing clusters and hail north of the front. MDs documented supercells and a later squall line, with prior convection and capping keeping confidence more conditional in some corridors.

boundary_drivers: sharp warm front from northern Illinois into Lower Michigan|Texas/Oklahoma dryline|cold front across Kansas/Missouri|surface low and strengthening low-level jet
storm_modes: intense warm-front supercells|dryline supercells|supercell clusters|bowing line segments|overnight QLCS
dominant_hazards: strong to intense tornadoes|very large to giant hail|damaging winds
day_narrative: This was a broad, multi-corridor MDT day from the southern Plains to the southern Great Lakes. The most focused tornado corridor was along the Midwest warm front, while Texas/Oklahoma dryline storms brought giant hail and tornado risk before transitioning toward linear wind-producing structures. MDs later showed several intense supercells and QLCS segments, preserving an all-hazards character deep into the night.

boundary_drivers: surging cold front|deep surface cyclone|prefrontal warm sector convergence|low-level jet
storm_modes: intense squall line|embedded supercells|warm-sector supercells|bowing line segments

day_narrative: A powerful cyclone and cold front produced a large lower/mid Mississippi Valley to Ohio Valley severe-wind episode. Outlooks emphasized widespread damaging winds with embedded tornadoes in a fast-moving squall line, while acknowledging a conditional strong-tornado risk in any storms that could stay ahead of the line. The threat persisted overnight into the Southeast as the line advanced eastward.

storm_modes: remnant and renewing QLCS|broken linear bands|supercell clusters|low-topped squall line

day_narrative: The day began as a Mid-Atlantic MDT for fast-moving storms, damaging winds, and possible strong long-track tornadoes. Ongoing broken lines, remnant QLCS activity, and large-scale outflow strongly limited destabilization and led to removal of the Moderate Risk by 20Z. Severe continued in several rounds, but the event was mainly a QLCS and low-topped wind/tornado regime rather than a cleaner discrete outbreak.

boundary_drivers: cold front from Ohio Valley into Mid-Atlantic|steep lapse-rate plume|prefrontal warm sector
storm_modes: initial discrete supercells|small bowing segments|elevated hail storms later

day_narrative: This Ohio Valley to Mid-Atlantic ENH was a steep-lapse-rate, cold-front severe hail and wind day. Moisture was limited, but surface heating was expected to erode inhibition and support discrete supercells at first. MDs favored severe hail and damaging gusts, with a tornado possible but not the main hazard.

boundary_drivers: southward-moving cold front|weak surface wave along southern Great Lakes front|lake breeze boundaries|subtle northwest-flow shortwave

day_narrative: A fast northwest-flow disturbance and southward-moving front supported severe storms from the Midwest into the Ohio Valley. The main signal was supercell hail, including greater than 2 inch stones, with damaging winds and a conditional tornado risk near better low-level shear and lake-breeze effects. Some storms became elevated as the front undercut the warm sector.

boundary_drivers: southern Plains dryline/front intersection|retreating warm front into Oklahoma/Kansas/Missouri|stationary boundary in the Ohio Valley|mesolow/MCV over western Oklahoma
dominant_hazards: damaging winds|large to very large hail|tornadoes
day_narrative: Southern Plains storms initiated along a broad front/dryline zone and then grew upscale as forcing increased. Supercells and clusters brought all hazards, with the 01Z outlook emphasizing a southwest Oklahoma complex aided by a mesolow/MCV. The Ohio Valley/Mid-Atlantic had a secondary frontal wind/hail risk, making the day multi-region and mixed-mode.

boundary_drivers: deep surface low tracking across Iowa|northward-lifting warm front|advancing cold front|midlevel dry slot
storm_modes: fast-moving supercells|bowing segment near the surface low|clusters|line segments
dominant_hazards: tornadoes including strong fast-moving tornadoes|damaging winds|hail
day_narrative: A negatively tilted trough and rapidly moving low created a narrow warm-sector recovery corridor across Iowa, Illinois, and southern Wisconsin. Strong low-level shear near the warm front favored fast supercells and a tornado threat, while bowing segments and clusters added damaging-wind potential. The main uncertainty was whether weak buoyancy after morning precipitation would be enough for sustained mature storms.

boundary_drivers: warm front from Missouri into Iowa/Illinois|surface low and triple point|advancing cold front|dryline/Pacific front into Oklahoma and Texas
storm_modes: warm-front supercells|cold-front line|discrete to semi-discrete supercells|expansive MCS

MDs later documented a transition to wind swaths and an expansive MCS, with outflow modulating the remaining tornado risk.

day_narrative: The primary severe risk focused on the Upper Mississippi Valley warm front, where late-day supercells were expected to produce large to very large hail and tornadoes. A conditional southern Plains dryline risk provided a separate all-hazards corridor if storms could sustain. The main uncertainty was storm residence time near the boundary versus rapid clustering north of the front.

day_narrative: This was a highly convectively modulated Plains-to-Great Lakes day. The Midwest ENH corridor formed along a composite outflow/warm-front zone, while southern Plains dryline supercells produced giant hail before cold pools and clustering shifted hazards toward wind. MDs repeatedly tied tornado and hail corridors to outflow, warm fronts, and MCV/cold-pool interactions.

day_narrative: A broad Midwest-to-Plains MDT began with supercells capable of giant hail and strong tornadoes, then evolved toward a damaging-wind-dominant MCS/QLCS. The southern Plains/lower Missouri Valley corridor had the clearest forward-propagating MCS signal, with 80+ mph gust potential. Farther north, warm-front supercells transitioned into a broken line with embedded mesovortices and severe wind.

day_narrative: A frontal severe corridor stretched from Minnesota/Iowa southward into Kansas and Oklahoma, with mixed modes along and ahead of the cold front. The more substantial evening threat focused from eastern Kansas into Oklahoma, where supercells produced very large hail and tornado potential before some upscale growth. Oklahoma dryline initiation remained conditional but potentially high-end if sustained.

day_narrative: The ENH risk was anchored to an outflow-dominated corridor from southeast Oklahoma into the ArkLaTex. Heating south of a morning convective band and its stalling/modifying outflow supported intense supercells with very large hail and tornado risk, while parts of the line could re-intensify into a QLCS wind/tornado threat. The Texas dryline was a separate, more conditional hail-focused risk.

day_narrative: A volatile southern Plains MDT focused on the warm front/outflow boundary and dryline intersection in Oklahoma and north Texas. Extreme buoyancy and steep lapse rates supported giant hail, with the strongest tornado risk tied to discrete, boundary-anchored supercells. Elevated supercells and clusters continued into the night, but storm interactions and cold pools complicated the dominant hazard corridor.

MDs showed MCSs and outflow zones shaping both the wind threat and renewed supercell/tornado potential.

By 01Z, a persistent convective system with embedded and preceding supercells was ongoing, with tornado potential still possible but not as cleanly realized as the earlier forecast suggested.

MDs confirmed intense tornadic supercells, followed by a more complicated convective environment with clusters and bowing segments.

Supercells developed near and north of the boundary with large hail and a tornado risk, then merged into a south-southeast-moving bowing MCS. By evening, the hazard profile shifted toward corridors of 75+ mph wind across central Texas while very large hail persisted with dominant supercell structures.

The strongest Plains wind corridor depended on timing of upscale growth and how storms interacted with the stalled front and modifying outflow.

MDs documented both a strong tornado with maturing Nebraska supercells and later severe-wind/QLCS tornado swaths as storms consolidated.

day_narrative: This MDT day focused on intense central Plains/Mid-Missouri Valley supercells along a retreating outflow boundary and cold-front triple point. Very unstable air and strong shear supported strong to intense tornadoes and giant hail before storms grew upscale into clusters and a squall line. A separate Great Lakes MCS and its cold pool strongly reduced recovery downstream, while the Oklahoma/Texas dryline remained more conditional.
